• # The Keeping of Light

  Mara Voss came back to Widow's Point in October, three weeks after her father's funeral, because the lighthouse would not stop writing to her. Not
  letters, exactly. The estate lawyer handed her a cardboard box of her father's effects, and inside, beneath a wool cap that still smelled of pipe
  smoke, sat the light's logbook. The Coast Guard had decommissioned the station eleven years ago; the lamp was automated now, a stubborn electric eye
  that blinked without opinion. But her father had kept logging anyway, every day for eleven years, in his narrow draftsman's hand. The entries
  stopped on September 14th — four days before he died — and Mara would have believed that was grief or sloppiness if the last entry hadn't said:
  Visitor coming. My daughter. Tell her about the fog. She won't believe me. She'll be right not to.

  She drove up the coast in her father's borrowed truck with the box riding shotgun like a relative she owed money to. The turnoff was unmarked, the
  way it had been when she was a child and the road was gravel and the world ended at the keeper's gate. Now the road was paved halfway and abandoned
  the rest of the way, asphalt surrendering to rutted dirt, and the tower rose out of the October fog the way it always had — sudden, white,
  ridiculous, like something a child had drawn and the world had agreed to keep.

  Her father had named her after nothing. "Names should be doors, not plaques," he used to say, which was the kind of thing a lighthouse keeper could
  afford to believe because he would never have to fit his philosophy on a business card. Mara had spent thirty-two years walking through doors he
  opened and never once asking where they led. She was a structural engineer in Seattle. She signed other people's bridges. She measured everything
  twice and trusted nothing once.

  The early volumes were ordinary. Weather, lamp hours, paint inventory, the small wars between gulls and her father's patience. Her mother appeared
  in them as a bright recurring character, then faded, then stopped — the year of the diagnosis, the year of the absence, the year Mara stopped coming
  up because coming up meant watching a man get smaller against a background that never got smaller. She read her own name twice in 2019 and had to
  set the book down. Daughter called. She is measuring something in Seattle. Told her you cannot plumb what refuses to be still. She said that's why
  we use statistics. I said that's why we drown.

  Then, in the 2023 volume, the entries changed.

  They were still in her father's hand. The ink was the same, the pressure the same, the little caret marks he used for wind direction the same. But
  the dates were wrong. Not missing, not skipped — ahead. The entry for October 3rd described weather that hadn't happened, a storm that arrived, she
  checked her phone, exactly on schedule. October 9th predicted a seal on the lower rocks, and on October 9th there was a seal on the lower rocks, fat
  and presumptuous, exactly where the log said it would haul out at 0700. Her father's handwriting had begun arriving before his days did.

  Mara was a structural engineer. She believed in load paths and safety factors and the incorruptible arithmetic of the physical world. She did not
